title: How to run Evals at Scale: Thinking beyond Accuracy or Similarity — Muktesh Mishra, Adobe
talk_summary: A short practitioner talk arguing that AI applications need eval suites built from labeled, multi-flow datasets, with eval types chosen per application (accuracy/similarity for Q&A, functional correctness for code, trajectory and multi-turn simulation for agents). It gives process guidance (measure-monitor-analyze-repeat, parallel orchestration, human-vs-automation tradeoff) but no concrete tooling, numbers, or measured results.

takeaways.technique: Per-artifact eval types instead of one universal score
takeaways.what_they_do: Choose eval metrics by output type: similarity/accuracy for Q&A, functional correctness and robustness against the real codebase for generated code, trajectory and tool-call correctness for agents.
For agent flows, evaluate the path taken (which steps/tools were invoked) rather than only the final output, because agents can reach the same output via different paths.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one of the important aspect for evaluating agents is trajectory evaluation because agents can take a different path

takeaways.technique: Multiple labeled datasets per flow, start synthetic
takeaways.what_they_do: Begin with small synthetic datasets, label them by flow/application aspect, and maintain separate datasets per flow rather than one big set; continuously fold observed outputs back in.
takeaways.evidence_quote: one data set is never sufficient. So when you are thinking about ewell you need to think about multiple data sets based on the flows

takeaways.what_they_do: Analogous to TDD: define evals from use cases (positive and negative cases) up front so prompt/model changes can be checked for regressions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you think about typical software like testdriven development this is the eval development define ewells based on the use cases

takeaways.technique: Parallel eval orchestration with intermediate-result capture
takeaways.what_they_do: Scale evals by capturing intermediate results and regressions, orchestrating/parallelizing eval runs, aggregating results, and running frequently in a measure-monitor-analyze-repeat loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can catch the intermediate results and regression. You need to focus on orchestration and parallelism

takeaways.what_they_do: Explicitly balance high-speed automated evals against high-fidelity human review depending on what is being checked, and rely on defined process over tools since not everything can be automated.
takeaways.evidence_quote: there is a fine balance or trade-off between human in the loop versus automation like whether you want the high speed versus high fidelity
